# Exploring Joyful Language in Jane Austen's Emma using Tidytext

## 1. Load libraries

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.height = 3,
  fig.width = 5
)

ggplot2::theme_set(
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white")
    )
)
```

```{r libraries, message=FALSE}
# Load the packages
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(janeaustenr)
library(wordcloud)
library(RColorBrewer)
```

## 2. Data Preparation

First, we load the Jane Austen books and prepare the data. We create a line number and chapter number for each line of text. Then we select Emma.

```{r data-preparation}
# Load Jane Austen's books
austen_data <- austen_books()

# Add line numbers and chapter numbers
austen_data <- austen_data %>%
  group_by(book) %>%
  mutate(
    linenumber = row_number(),
    chapter = cumsum(
      str_detect(
        text,
        regex("^chapter\\s+[0-9ivxlc]+", ignore_case = TRUE)
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Select Emma
emma <- austen_data %>%
  filter(book == "Emma")

# Show the first few rows
head(emma)
```

The `austen_books()` function loads Jane Austen's books. We group the data by book and identify chapter headings using regular expressions. The line number and chapter number are added as new columns.


## 3. Tokenization

Use `unnest_tokens()` to separate the text into individual words. This allows to compare the words in the novel with the sentiment lexicons.

```{r tokenization}
# Separate the text into individual words
emma_words <- emma %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

# Display the first few words
head(emma_words)
```

Each row now represents one word from the novel. The words are converted to lowercase automatically, making it easier to match them with the sentiment lexicons.



## 4. NRC Sentiment Analysis

The NRC sentiment lexicon classifies words into different emotions. This analysis focuse on words associated with joy.

```{r nrc-analysis}
# Load the NRC lexicon and select joyful words
nrc_joy <- get_sentiments("nrc") %>%
  filter(sentiment == "joy")

# Match joyful words with words from Emma
emma_nrc <- emma_words %>%
  inner_join(nrc_joy, by = "word")

# Count the frequency of each word
nrc_frequency <- emma_nrc %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  filter(n > 50)

# Display the most frequent joyful words
nrc_frequency
```


### NRC Bar Chart

```{r nrc-bar-chart}
# Create a bar chart of frequent joyful words
ggplot(nrc_frequency, aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkseagreen3") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Frequent Joy Words in Emma (NRC)",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

The bar chart displays the most frequent joyful words identified by the NRC lexicon. The words are ordered by frequency to make comparisons easier.

### NRC Word Cloud

```{r nrc-word-cloud}
# Create a word cloud using NRC joyful words
wordcloud(
  words = nrc_frequency$word,
  freq = nrc_frequency$n,
  max.words = 100,
  random.order = FALSE,
  colors = brewer.pal(8, "Dark2")
)
```

The word cloud provides another way to visualize the results. Words that appear more frequently are displayed in larger sizes.
